newsitem.title: FRANCE: France probes Credit Foncier irregularities.
newsitem.headline: France probes Credit Foncier irregularities.

text.p: French public prosecutors have launched an inquiry into alleged financial irregularities at the troubled property loans group Credit Foncier between 1992 and 1994, government spokesman Alain Lamassoure said on Wednesday.

"An investigation is under way...on counts of distributing ficticious dividends, presenting inaccurate accounts and illegal conflict of interest covering 1992, 1993 and 1994 at Credit Foncier. Justice will be done," he told the National Assembly.

The inquiry is the latest twist in a tale of intrigue and financial disaster which has prompted a plan to "nationalise" the group and wind it down after nearly 150 years in business, despite resistance from staff, unions and politicians.

Former chairman Jean-Claude Colli, named by late Socialist President Francois Mitterand in 1994, was ousted in January by the current centre-right government and Jerome Meyssonier sent in to replace him.

While the group was private and listed on the stock market, the government was in charge of appointing top managers because of Credit Foncier's role in providing low-cost housing loans on behalf of the state.

In April, it announced a 1995 loss of 10.8 billion francs ($2.1 billion) after registering provisions of 13.6 billion for its exposure to the property market which collapsed at the end of the 1980s. The affair quickly took on national importance.

Finance Minister Jean Arthuis told parliament there had been "reckless errors" in the past, that the Paris prosecutor had been asked to take up the case and that he was giving Meyssonier until the end of July to find a buyer or face shut-down.
"The loss of 11 billion francs we see today is because, at the end of the 1980s and the start of the 1990s, Credit Foncier got involved in reckless investments," Arthuis said at the time.
"I would like to say that chairman Meyssonier has, as of now, taken the matter to the state prosector's office so that any illegal actions can be sanctioned by the law."

Meyssonier's search for a buyer came to nothing and Arthuis announced a plan in July to gradually wind Credit Foncier down, starting with a buyout of shareholders by the state-owned bank Caisse des Depots et Consignations (CDC).
The CDC has now carried out the takeover at the government's behest and Arthuis has to decide whether to proceed with the next step of his plan.
But the group has since reported a profit for the first half of the year and Meyssonier says a profit of one billion francs in 1996 is possible.

The predictions have injected new life into a campaign by 3,500 staff, unions and politicians who say the state is partly to blame for the errors of the past and that Arthuis should seek another solution for a group they say is viable.
The National Assembly's influential finance committee was also considering on Wednesday whether to set up a parliamentary commission of inquiry into Credit Foncier.
